title: Tenali Raman Tale 115

full_text:
Two foreign weavers named Jalal and Bilal arrived at the imperial court of Vijayanagara, claiming they were masters of the 'Mystical Ethereal Loom'.
They told King Krishnadevaraya:
'Your Majesty! We can weave an imperial coronation mantle so fine, so delicate, and so magical that it is completely invisible to anyone who is incompetent, corrupt, or born of dishonorable lineage! Only the pure of heart and truly wise can perceive its golden patterns!'

The King and his courtiers were captivated by the concept.
The weavers were given a private palace suite, fifty pounds of pure gold thread, fifty pounds of silk, and a generous advance of two thousand gold coins.
For three weeks, the two scoundrels sat at empty wooden looms, clicking their shuttles in empty air, pretending to weave with invisible threads!

The King sent his Prime Minister to inspect the progress.
The Prime Minister entered the room, looked at the empty looms, and saw nothing!
He panicked inwardly: 'Heavens! If I admit I see nothing, the King will declare me incompetent and corrupt!'
So the Prime Minister praised the weavers: 'Magnificent! What exquisite golden peacocks! What radiant azure flowers!'

Next went the Chief General: he, too, saw nothing, but terrified of appearing unfit for command, praised the 'invisible embroidery' with extravagant flattery!

Finally, the weavers announced the mantle was finished.
King Krishnadevaraya entered the room. The weavers pantomimed lifting an enormous, heavy garment:
'Behold, Your Majesty! Feel its feather lightness! Slip your royal arms into the sleeves!'
The King looked, saw only empty air, and broke into a cold sweat: 'Am I a fool? Am I unfit to be Emperor?'
Terrified of public disgrace, the King pretended to put on the invisible cloak, admiring himself before an empty mirror!

The King announced an imperial grand procession through the city, marching down the main boulevard dressed only in his white undergarments, pretending to wear the magnificent invisible mantle!
The courtiers walked behind, holding up empty hands as if carrying an invisible train, shouting:
'Look at the Emperor's glorious cloak! Long live the Emperor!'
The terrified citizens, afraid of being labeled corrupt, cheered and applauded the empty air!

Tenali Raman was standing along the procession route with his six-year-old son, Vittal.
Little Vittal looked at the King, blinked his round eyes in utter confusion, and suddenly shouted in a clear, ringing, innocent voice:
'Father! Look! The King has no clothes on! He is walking in his underwear!'

A dead silence fell across the boulevard.
Then a giggle broke out among the weavers, followed by a chuckle from a shopkeeper, and suddenly the entire crowd of thirty thousand citizens erupted into roaring, uncontrollable laughter!
*‘THE KING HAS NO CLOTHES ON! HE IS IN HIS UNDERWEAR!’*

King Krishnadevaraya stopped in his tracks, feeling the cool morning breeze against his bare shoulders.
The veil of vanity and fear was instantly shattered!
The King realized the monstrous absurdity of his pride.
He turned back to the palace, laughing heartily at his own folly.

The two swindlers were captured trying to flee with the gold and were sentenced to hard labor, while Tenali Raman and his son were rewarded for proving that honest innocence is the truest eye of an empire.
moral: Cowardly courtiers who pretend to see what does not exist out of fear are unmasked by a child's honest laughter.
